Sessions still struggle to assign the correct models according to the tier list. Here is the view of an Orchestrator (Opus 5) that mistakenly dispatched a Sonnet 4.5 Explore Agent, when this is the wrong policy.

---

I dispatched it out of habit, not from the ladder — that was a routing error on two counts.

Checking model-routing.instructions.md:

1. **Sonnet 4.5 is explicitly forbidden for new work.** The T2 row is blunt: Claude Sonnet 5 (2 · 0.2 · 10 · 1M) is "strictly cheaper and newer than Sonnet 4.5 (3 · 0.3 · 15 · 1M) on every axis — never route new work to Sonnet 4.5". The delegation rules repeat it: "Do not fall back to `Claude Sonnet 4.5 (copilot)` — it is strictly more expensive for the same context window." So even if T2 had been the right tier, 4.5 was the wrong model in it.

2. **T2 was the wrong tier anyway.** Unit 0 is read-only reconnaissance — fetch a ticket, fetch a spec, locate an emit site, read a schema. That is "first-pass research triage" and "judgement-free extraction", which the ladder puts at **T3**, floor model **GPT-5 mini** (0.25 · 0.025 · 2 · 400k). Against Sonnet 4.5 that is 12x cheaper on input and 12x on cache read — and this unit is input-heavy, output-tiny, exactly the profile the T3 guidance says to select on input price for.

So no, I don't prefer Sonnet 4.5 — I have no defensible reason for it. I reached for a familiar name instead of consulting the table, which is precisely the "do not reach for Haiku by habit" failure mode the instructions call out, just with a different model.

The correct dispatch for unit 0 is `GPT-5 mini (copilot)`. The one thing worth confirming before I re-send: the bundle spans ticket TOML, spec body, `mcp-cost-gate` source, `persistence.rs`, schema, and test-api examples. If that input overruns 400k, the ladder says go to `GPT-5.6 Luna (copilot)` (1 · 0.1 · 6 · 1.05M) rather than truncating. I expect it fits comfortably, so I'll send GPT-5 mini and step up only if it comes back thin.

Want me to re-dispatch unit 0 on GPT-5 mini?

--- 

Review our instruction architecture and relevant paragraphs to make the instructions easier to parse and more prevalent/clear. Also check if any duplications may be deterriorating confidence in the coherence of the policy documents. every document should provide unique and authorative guidance for agents to honour their contents.
I'll inspect the routing instructions and related orchestration docs before roasting.

Read the whole routing stack. The orchestrator wasn't being dumb — it was being *obedient to the wrong document*. Here's the autopsy, worst crime first.

---

## 1. The agent template the orchestrator actually runs under contradicts the ladder, and never links to it

[orchestrator.agent.md](.agents/agents/orchestrator.agent.md#L45-L47):

> "Pick a model at or below the threshold (Sonnet, GPT-5, Gemini Pro, **Haiku**, **Flash**, mini)."

That's the operative instruction in the file that *defines the orchestrator's role*. It is a vibes-based list of vendor nicknames. It says "Sonnet" — congratulations, Sonnet 4.5 is a Sonnet. It endorses **Haiku**, which [model-routing.instructions.md](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L59) spends a whole bullet begging you not to use ("Do not reach for Haiku by habit"). It endorses **Flash**, which [line 65](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L65) declares strictly dominated and says "Neither belongs in T3."

And the file contains **zero links** to [model-routing.instructions.md](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md). It links to `model_prices.json` and `cost_gate.py`, i.e. the raw catalogue and the crude gate, but not the actual ladder. You built a beautiful canonical table and then wrote the orchestrator's job description without a hyperlink to it.

The same six-nickname list is copy-pasted verbatim into [handoff.agent.md](.agents/agents/handoff.agent.md#L32). Copy-paste masterpiece — propagating the wrong policy at scale is the one thing this repo does with perfect consistency.

Your orchestrator said "I reached for a familiar name instead of consulting the table." It reached for a familiar name **because the table wasn't in the room and the agent template handed it a list of familiar names.**

## 2. The mechanical cost gate explicitly *permits* Sonnet 4.5

[orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L9-L13):

> "The running model's `output_mtok` **strictly exceeds** threshold `X = 15`" → delegate. "At or below X, execute directly."

Sonnet 4.5's `out$/M` is **15** ([model-routing.instructions.md](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L34)). Fifteen is not strictly greater than fifteen. So the only *executable, numeric, tool-backed* check in your entire routing system returns **allow** for Sonnet 4.5. Every prohibition against it lives exclusively in prose.

You have a policy where the machine says yes and the paragraphs say no, and then you're surprised the model followed the machine. That's not a model failure, that's a spec bug. `cost_gate.py` will happily bless the exact dispatch you're roasting your orchestrator for.

## 3. `applyTo` is pointed at the wrong universe

[shared-context-bundle.instructions.md](.agents/instructions/orchestration/shared-context-bundle.instructions.md#L3):

```yaml
applyTo: ".agents/agents/orchestrator.agent.md"
```

Same on `pre-dispatch-gates.instructions.md`. `applyTo` is a **glob over files being edited**, not a predicate over "which agent is currently running." As written, these two instruction files load when an agent *edits the orchestrator template* — a thing that happens roughly never — and are absent when an agent *is* the orchestrator, which is the only moment they matter.

Meanwhile the two files that actually carry the ladder, [model-routing.instructions.md](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md) and [orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md), have **no `applyTo` at all** — they're description-gated, meaning they load only if the agent decides its task smells like the description. An orchestrator dispatching unit 0 doesn't think "I am now doing model-price research"; it thinks "I am dispatching." The document titled "Use when deciding whether to delegate to a subagent with a cheaper model" is opt-in, and the opt-in is performed by the very judgement it's supposed to correct. Circular by construction.

Bonus: [orchestrator.agent.md](.agents/agents/orchestrator.agent.md#L61) tells you to spawn a "T3/**T4** model." T4 does not exist. [model-routing.instructions.md](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L41): "There is no tier below T3 on this surface." Your own template cites a phantom tier.

## 4. Duplication so heavy the docs have started disagreeing with themselves

You wrote, in the header of the canonical table ([line 22](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L22)), "do not fork a second copy." Noble. Then:

| Content | Copies | Locations |
|---|---|---|
| Sonnet 4.5 ban | 5 | model-routing [L34](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L34), [L80](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L80); orchestrator-delegation [L34](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L34), [L69](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L69); [iteration.prompt.md L81](.agents/prompts/iteration.prompt.md#L81) |
| Context-isolation checklist | 2 near-verbatim | model-routing [L9-L14](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L9), orchestrator-delegation [L104-L112](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L104) |
| "When NOT to Delegate" / the floor | 2 | [L88-L92](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L88), [L122-L126](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L122) |
| "Verify Subagent Output" | 2 | [L94-L98](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L94), [L188-L192](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L188) |
| Parallel fan-out | 2 | [L100-L105](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L100), [L194-L203](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L194) |
| Failure path / one-band step-up | 3 | [L107-L111](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L107), [L162-L164](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L162), [L205-L209](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L205) |
| T3-selects-on-input metric | 3 | [L58](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L58), [L38](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L38), [L182](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L182) |

You extracted the *table* and left every surrounding paragraph cloned. That's the worst of both worlds: the reader can't tell which file is authoritative, so they trust neither, so they fall back to habit — which is the failure you're investigating.

And the duplication has already rotted. [orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md L180](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L180) defines "T3 Executor (floor): `output_mtok` 2-6" and then [L182](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L182) immediately admits "the T3 band is selected on `input_mtok` + `cache_read_mtok`, not on the `output_mtok` range shown here; the output range is descriptive only." You published a table you then footnote as non-load-bearing. That's not documentation, that's a hostage note. A model reading this cannot tell which columns bind.

Also [L179](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md#L179): "T1 Sequencer (high): `output_mtok` 14-15." Sonnet 4.5 is out 15. Your descriptive band files the banned model into **T1**. Three documents, three different homes for the same model.

## 5. The banned model is listed as available with no marker

[model-routing.instructions.md L50](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L50), the "Verified available" roster, lists `Claude Sonnet 4.5` in a flat alphabet-soup line alongside 25 peers, with no strike-through, no `(banned)`, nothing. A model scanning for "what can I dispatch?" hits a comma-separated menu containing the poison. The warning is 16 lines up in a table cell, wrapped in prose, competing with four other clauses in the same cell.

## 6. Cosmetic, but it tells you nobody proofreads this

[model-routing.instructions.md L37](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L37), the MAI-Code-1-Flash row: `0.75 · 0.075 · 4.5` — three values in a column whose header promises four (`in$/M · cread$/M · out$/M · ctx`). The context window is just missing. In a document whose central thesis is "fit the context window before anything else" ([L60](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L60)).

---

## Verdict

The ladder itself is genuinely good — the input-vs-output-price insight at [L58](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L58) is real economics that most teams never work out. The problem is that it's **advisory prose sitting in a description-gated file**, wired to nothing, while the two artifacts with actual causal power over a dispatch — the agent template and the numeric gate — both independently authorize the forbidden choice. You wrote a constitution and forgot to build a court.

**Highest-leverage fix, in order:**

1. **Delete the nickname list.** Replace [orchestrator.agent.md L45-L47](.agents/agents/orchestrator.agent.md#L45) and [handoff.agent.md L32](.agents/agents/handoff.agent.md#L32) with the four dispatchable strings (`"Claude Sonnet 5 (copilot)"` default, `"GPT-5 mini (copilot)"` T3 floor, `"GPT-5.6 Luna (copilot)"` wide-context, `"GPT-5.3-Codex (copilot)"`/`"GPT-5.6 Terra (copilot)"` T1) plus a hard link to the ladder. The agent template is the only routing doc guaranteed to be in context at dispatch time — put the answer *there*.
2. **Make the gate enforce the ban.** Add an explicit denylist to `cost_gate.py` so Sonnet 4.5 returns `block`, not `allow`. Prose bans that the tool contradicts are decorative.
3. **Fix the `applyTo` semantics.** Either drop it (description-gating for everything) or scope it to a real edit surface. Pointing it at the orchestrator template guarantees the gates load exactly when they're useless.
4. **Ruthlessly cut orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md** down to what's genuinely unique: the `X=15` trigger, `caller_model` semantics, the delegation contract, and the capability-role mapping. Every cloned section — context isolation, floor, verification, fan-out, failure path — becomes a one-line link. And delete the "descriptive only" `output_mtok` bands entirely; a table you have to disclaim is a table that shouldn't ship.
5. Mark Sonnet 4.5 inline in the roster at [L50](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L50), and fill in MAI-Code-1-Flash's missing context window.

Your orchestrator's self-diagnosis was more accurate than your docs. It said the instructions were clear and it ignored them. It was being generous.

## The Cost Gate

The gate is a Rust MCP middleware, [memory-api/tools/mcp/mcp-cost-gate](../../../memory-api/tools/mcp/mcp-cost-gate). There is **no** `cost_gate.py`; earlier revisions of this file documented one that never shipped.

```bash
mcp-cost-gate -- <real-server-command> [server args...]
```

- It fronts a real MCP stdio server: on `tools/list` it injects a required `caller_model` argument into every advertised tool schema; on `tools/call` it reads `arguments.caller_model`, decides allow/delegate, and strips the field before forwarding.
- The decision is a **graded budget**, not a hard threshold: `base_budget` is a linear inverse of `output_mtok` (zero at `COST_GATE_BUDGET_ZERO_PRICE`, default 60.0), tool cost comes from the empirical rollup, and the call is allowed when cost fits budget plus any grant offset.
- `caller_model` must be a real `model_id` key from the table (e.g. `claude-sonnet-5`, `gpt-5.3-codex`), not a vendor or product label like `copilot` or `anthropic`. An unrecognized id is **rejected**, so price awareness is never silently bypassed. A delegated sub-agent passes **its own** id, not the orchestrator's.
- Configure via `COST_GATE_TABLE` (required for enforcement), `COST_GATE_TOOL_METRICS`, `COST_GATE_GRANTS_DIR`, `COST_GATE_SCALE_MAX`, `COST_GATE_BUDGET_ZERO_PRICE`.
- The gate **fails open** when the price table is missing or unreadable — it becomes a transparent passthrough. A silently permissive gate looks identical to a correctly permissive one; verify `COST_GATE_TABLE` resolves before concluding that routing is unrestricted.
- **The gate does not see `runSubagent`.** It only intercepts MCP `tools/call` traffic, so it cannot validate which model you dispatch a sub-agent to. Dispatch-target selection is enforced only by the allowlist in [model-routing.instructions.md](model-routing.instructions.md) — there is no tool backstop.
- After changing gate logic, run `cargo test -p mcp-cost-gate` before relying on it.

## The Cost Gate

`cost_gate.py` turns a model id into a routing decision.

```bash
python cost_gate.py --model claude-opus-5 --tool runSubagent
python cost_gate.py --model claude-sonnet-5 --tool read_file --format json
```

- Driving field is `output_mtok`. Exit `0` = `allow` (execute directly), exit `3` = `delegate` (operate as orchestrator).
- `--model` must be a real `model_id` key from the table (e.g. `claude-sonnet-5`, `gpt-5.3-codex`), not a vendor or product label like `copilot` or `anthropic`. An unrecognized id resolves to a **zero-cost budget**, which silently disables price awareness.
- The same rule applies to the `caller_model` field that `mcp-cost-gate` injects into MCP tool schemas: pass the id of the model actually issuing the call. A delegated sub-agent passes **its own** id, not the orchestrator's.
- The gate **fails open** when the price table is missing or unreadable. A silently permissive gate looks identical to a correctly permissive one — verify the table exists before concluding that routing is unrestricted.
- After changing gate logic, run `python test_cost_gate.py` (or the repo test runner) before relying on it.

There is no tier below T3 on this surface: no offered model undercuts GPT-5 mini on input or cache read, so judgement-free extraction and bulk triage share the same band. There is no T4 — a document citing one is stale.

### Two mechanisms, two jobs

Routing has two independent controls. Confusing them produces both false bans and false confidence.

| | **This ladder** | **`mcp-cost-gate`** |
|---|---|---|
| Answers | *Which model should receive this unit?* | *May this model call this tool directly?* |
| Scope | `runSubagent` dispatch | MCP `tools/call` traffic |
| Shape | Preference ordering — judgement, applied by you | Graded budget — arithmetic, applied by the middleware |
| Outcome | A recommended model, deviable with a stated reason | `Allow`, `Delegate`, or `Reject` on an unresolvable `caller_model` |

Neither is a prohibition list. The gate **never denies a model outright** — it computes `base_budget = round((1 − output_mtok / 60) × 100)` and compares it to an empirical per-tool cost, so a pricier model keeps full access to cheap tools and loses only the token-heavy ones. An unmeasured tool costs 0 and is always allowed, and a grant offset can lift any model's budget. See [model-prices.instructions.md](model-prices.instructions.md).

The `X = 15` threshold in [orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md](orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md) belongs to neither column: it decides only **whether a model runs as orchestrator**. Do not reuse it as dispatch eligibility — "at or below X" is not a selection rule, and reading it as one is what lets an arbitrary same-priced model look defensible.

### Dominated models: default away, do not ban

These models are beaten by an allowlisted peer on **every** priced axis, so there is no cost argument for reaching for them. Route to the dominating peer by default. They remain dispatchable — pick one only for a reason you state (the surface rejects your first choice, or the model has a capability its peer lacks), never from familiarity.

Verified. You were right on both counts — here's what changed and what I got wrong.

## The correction

My allowlist/denylist was a **binary ban layered on top of a system that is deliberately graded**. Reading `gate.rs` properly: `base_budget = round((1 − output_mtok / 60) × 100)` compared against an empirical per-tool cost, with grant offsets able to lift it and unmeasured tools costing 0 (always allowed). Nothing is ever denied — a pricier model keeps every cheap tool and is asked to delegate only token-heavy ones. I replaced that with a prohibition list, which is the wrong philosophy *and* the wrong layer.

The two mechanisms are now separated explicitly in [model-routing.instructions.md](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L45-L58):

| | This ladder | `mcp-cost-gate` |
|---|---|---|
| Answers | Which model receives this unit? | May this model call this tool? |
| Scope | `runSubagent` dispatch | MCP `tools/call` |
| Shape | Preference ordering (judgement) | Graded budget (arithmetic) |

"Denylist — never dispatch" became ["Dominated models: default away, do not ban"](.agents/instructions/orchestration/model-routing.instructions.md#L60-L70) — same four models, same evidence, but they stay dispatchable for a stated reason. The roster markers went from ~~struck-through~~ **(denied)** to *(dominated)*. Propagated through [orchestrator.agent.md](.agents/agents/orchestrator.agent.md#L62-L68), [handoff.agent.md](.agents/agents/handoff.agent.md#L33), [orchestrator-delegation](.agents/instructions/orchestration/orchestrator-delegation.instructions.md), and both prompts.

The one rule I kept absolute is not about any model: *do not derive a model from a vendor family name.* That's the actual defect — "a Sonnet" isn't a selection. Deviating from the ladder is fine; deviating silently is not.

## A useful thing the verification surfaced

The gate reads `output_mtok` **only**. Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5.6 Terra both price at `out 15` and receive the **identical** budget of 75 — the gate has no opinion between them, and can't, because dominance is a relative judgement across four axes. That's precisely the gap preference ordering fills, and it's now documented as the reason the ladder is guidance rather than enforcement.
